shared: The Aston-Martin Fiver series represents the flagship product line of a small luxury automaker based in Connery, a port city on the peaceful Federated Suns world of Numenor. Produced beginning in 3064, the current Fiver models are battery-powered electric vehicles designed to appeal to Numenor's wealthy noble class, whose cultural values prize environmentally responsible and quiet transportation above combustion alternatives. The series consists of two complementary models, the compact two-seat Roadster aimed at performance-minded buyers and the larger eight-passenger Traveler targeting family and group transport. Both vehicles share a common electric drivetrain philosophy and are marketed together as a cohesive product family, with Aston-Martin positioning the pair as the definitive luxury vehicle choice for sophisticated buyers on Numenor and, the company hopes, across the broader Federated Suns.

Aston-Martin has operated in Connery for generations predating the formation of the Federated Commonwealth, producing high-end vehicles for Numenor's noble class. The citizens of Numenor, insulated from the worst of the Succession Wars by their world's long peaceful history, developed a distinctive culture of wealth, erudition, and political consciousness that made battery-powered electric vehicles an obvious choice for the socially aware buyer. Combustion engines were seen as both polluting and politically retrograde, and the quiet operation of electric motors appealed even to those whose interest in environmental policy was primarily social rather than principled. Earlier Aston-Martin models catered to this sentiment and helped establish the brand as the aspirational choice for Numenoran elites.

The emergence of the Federated Commonwealth brought broader market competition to Numenor's luxury vehicle sector. Avanti hover vehicles produced in the Lyran Alliance aggressively expanded into Federated Suns markets during the FedCom era, capturing significant share through a campaign that linked Avanti ownership to political loyalty to the Archon. The strategy proved effective enough to displace Aston-Martin from New Avalon entirely, as Lyran-leaning buyers purchased Avanti vehicles to signal alignment with the Steiner half of the Commonwealth. Aston-Martin retreated to its Numenoran home market during this period, continuing sales of existing models while absorbing the competitive damage.

The FedCom Civil War reversed this dynamic. As Davion pride resurged and sentiment against Lyran-origin products grew across the Federated Suns, Aston-Martin moved quickly to capitalize. The company introduced the Fiver series in 3064, timing the launch to coincide with the cultural shift away from FedCom-era loyalties. The Roadster and Traveler were designed and marketed as a paired family, linked by a shared advertising campaign that explicitly positioned Avanti hover vehicles as the competition. Aston-Martin's marketing representatives compared the Fivers favorably to Avanti's latest models on range, comfort, and road-handling performance, arguing that wheeled electric vehicles were more practical for Numenor's developed road network than the hover technology favored in the Lyran Alliance. Three dealerships in Connery handle all Numenoran sales, and Aston-Martin salesmen are well known for their skill at appraising the social status of prospective buyers before tailoring their pitch accordingly.

shared: The Auxiliary Defense Tank emerged from political necessity following the Umayyad Caliphate's conquest of Castilian territories in 2830. Seeking to appease local nobles while keeping their forces outgunned, Umayyad administrators commissioned a fighting vehicle built around an existing earthmover chassis. Manufactured at several sites across Granada and Castile beginning in 2833, the ADT was never intended as a front-line warfighting machine. Its designers prioritized availability over performance, producing a vehicle that could be fielded quickly and cheaply, if not effectively. Crews and commanders alike regarded it with ambivalence, and it earned the Periphery nickname 'Oruga Negra,' the Black Caterpillar, a backhanded acknowledgment that while no individual tank posed a serious threat, enough of them together could still cause harm.

The ADT-1 is a 28-ton tracked vehicle powered by a Colonial Agricultural Standard 85 internal combustion engine, providing a top speed of 54 km/h, modest but compatible with the infantry-heavy formations that formed the backbone of Castilian and Umayyad ground forces. The Granada Guard Mk 2 armor meets only BAR 6 standards, offering adequate resistance to small arms but little comfort against dedicated anti-armor weapons. Its armament reflects the constraints of Periphery industry: a single medium rifle with two tons of ammunition provided the main punch, supplemented by a machine gun for anti-personnel work. In practice the machine gun saw heavier use, as the ADT was frequently deployed to suppress civil unrest rather than fight peer adversaries. The design carries Poor Workmanship and Unreliable quirks throughout its service life, reflecting the rushed conversion of agricultural machinery and persistent maintenance demands that frustrated crews.

The ADT-2 replaced the medium rifle with an AC/5 on a redesigned turret and incorporated an updated drivetrain allowing heavier armor protection. Introduced through Hanseatic League commercial distribution, the upgrade gave the design more credible anti-armor capability while preserving the fundamental chassis.

The Umayyad invasion of Castilian space in 2830 left the conquerors with a governance problem as much as a military one. Castilian nobles, fiercely proud and armed with personal retinues, represented a persistent insurgency risk that required careful management. The Umayyad solution was pragmatic: provide the nobles with a standardized fighting vehicle built from locally available agricultural machinery, giving them something to command while ensuring their forces remained outgunned by Umayyad regulars.

Production began at Caliphate Airfield Alpha and Pride of Granada Industries on Granada in 2833, with the design later replicated by the Castilians at King Dumount Defense Facility. From 2833 to 2862 the ADT-1 saw front-line service, first in skirmishes between rival Castilian noble houses and later as the Umayyads fractured into internal conflict. Unable to keep pace with escalating weapons technology, the ADT was pushed from front-line to garrison roles after 2862. The Castilians' own development of the Reconquista BattleMech ultimately made the ADT obsolete as a serious combat asset.

The ADT-2 arrived not through indigenous development but through commerce. The Hanseatic League recognized a market opportunity and began selling the upgraded variant to both sides of the Umayyad conflict around 2903. The simultaneous appearance of the same tank on opposing sides initially raised fears of espionage, but the commercial explanation emerged quickly. The AC/5 armament and improved drivetrain extended the design's useful service life, though it too was phased out by 2973 as more capable equipment arrived in the region.

text.overview: Clan Hell's Horses upgraded their standard Clan hoverpods with Omni technology, adding a larger engine to improve versatility and speed. The result was the Boreas, which can swap weaponry based on battlefield needs. It has since become the premier covert operations support vehicle for infantry scout units in the Horses' touman, providing fast, flexible reconnaissance with a two-seat crew arrangement.

shared: The Brunel Dump Truck is a massive large-wheeled support vehicle produced by Achernar Heavy Industries, first designed in 2637 to serve the ore extraction industry. Built around the demands of heavy strip-mining operations, the Brunel hauls enormous loads of raw ore and debris from extraction sites to processing facilities, handling work that would otherwise require multiple smaller vehicles. Although it competes against Earthwerks Incorporated's lighter Lesseps in overlapping markets, the Brunel's greater carrying capacity and economies of scale make it the preferred choice wherever mining volumes justify the investment in a larger machine. A distinctive subculture of heavy truck enthusiasts has grown up around the Brunel across the Inner Sphere, with racing and pulling competitions drawing drivers who modify their rigs well beyond factory specifications, a practice the manufacturer notes in its warranty documentation with conspicuous displeasure.

At one hundred fifty tons, the Brunel represents the heavy end of wheeled support vehicle design. Its petrochemical internal combustion engine delivers a maximum speed of fifty kilometers per hour, modest for its class but adequate for the roads and rough terrain typical of active mining sites. The vehicle mounts four tons of commercial-grade armor at a barrier armor rating of six, providing basic protection against incidental hazards without the weight penalty of military-grade materials. This level of protection is sufficient for the industrial environments the Brunel is designed to operate in, but offers little meaningful resistance to any organized weapons fire.

The Brunel's most significant specification is its cargo capacity, with a standard load rating of fifty tons in its rear dump box. Its off-road chassis and controls modification allows it to navigate the ungraded terrain common to active extraction operations, and a forward-mounted backhoe enables the vehicle to load ore and debris without relying on separate equipment. The combination of heavy carrying capacity, integrated loading capability, and off-road mobility makes the Brunel the dominant tool in large-scale surface extraction, though its slow speed and thin armor make it entirely unsuitable for any combat role.

The Chi-Ha Infantry Combat Vehicle is a primitive tracked troop transport produced by Daisho MilWorks of New Samarkand for the Draconis Combine. First entering military service in 2284, the Chi-Ha served as the primary infantry carrier for the early Combine military and was essential to the state's territorial expansion during the Age of War. Though eventually superseded by more advanced designs in front-line roles, the vehicle's simplicity and low cost kept it in Combine service through the Star League era, with limited production resuming during the Succession Wars to address persistent shortages of infantry transport capacity.

The Chi-Ha is a 22-ton tracked vehicle powered by an internal combustion engine that drives it to a maximum speed of 64 kilometers per hour across most terrain, with a range exceeding 1,000 kilometers. This combination of reasonable mobility and extended endurance suited the vehicle's original role as a military carrier across the Combine's varied worlds. Two tons of BAR 6 armor protect the crew and passengers against light arms fire, adequate for secondary support tasks but not intended for sustained engagement against armored opposition.

Three machine guns, two in a turret and one in the forward hull, share a single ton of ammunition. This arrangement provides overlapping coverage for suppressing infantry and light targets and for protecting the vehicle during troop embarkation and debarkation. The 3-ton infantry compartment accommodates a full platoon, who exit through two rear doors. The Low Profile design quirk reduces the vehicle's silhouette against incoming fire, a meaningful advantage in the urban and fortified environments where the Chi-Ha often operates.

The Original version from 2284 uses slightly reduced speed of 54 km/h and BAR 5 armor with a basic fire control system. The Standard version introduced in 2352 incorporates improved armor, advanced fire control, and the better speed rating, reflecting incremental improvements accumulated over nearly seven decades of service experience.

The Chi-Ha began its existence as a civilian cargo transport operating in the territories that would form the Draconis Combine. Daisho MilWorks of New Samarkand recognized the vehicle's practical qualities and undertook its conversion to a military troop transport, delivering the first military versions to the Planetary Militia in 2284. The timing aligned with the emergence of Shiro Kurita as a military and political force, and the Chi-Ha became one of the primary vehicles used to carry Combine infantry in the campaigns that brought new worlds under Kurita authority. As Shiro's ambitions expanded, Chi-Ha production spread to four additional worlds beyond New Samarkand to meet the growing army's transportation requirements.

The vehicle's front-line service life extended through the Age of War but began declining in the late twenty-fourth century as more capable designs entered production. The Chi-Ha was progressively reassigned to garrison, support, and training roles, where its simplicity and low maintenance overhead remained valuable. An improved version entering service in 2352 incorporated better armor and fire control, extending the design's operational relevance into the Star League era under what became the standard production model.

The Succession Wars and their attendant destruction of manufacturing capacity created recurring shortages of replacement transport vehicles across the Dragon's massive military structure. Daisho MilWorks periodically resumed limited Chi-Ha production runs to partially offset these shortages, as the vehicle's well-understood construction and minimal material requirements made it one of the easier designs to restart when other options were unavailable. The Chi-Ha's name, drawing on Japanese military nomenclature rooted in Combine tradition, reflects the cultural heritage that shaped the early Draconis state, an echo of ancient Terra preserved in the designation of one of the Combine's most durable military tools.

The Cobra VTOL Transport traces its origins to the formative years of the Terran Hegemony's military organization, commissioned from Pacific-Euro Consolidated Aerospace Systems on Terra in 2317. The design emerged from Director-General James McKenna's sweeping initiative to replace the fragmented procurement practices of the Alliance Global Militia with a standardized, purpose-built military equipment base. McKenna's vision demanded a light transport capable of operating across the full range of Hegemony operations, from battlefield resupply runs to rear-area logistics, and the tilt-rotor Cobra answered that specification with a design that proved both practical and adaptable. Capable of delivering troops, supplies, and light vehicles to contested forward positions and evacuating casualties on the return, the Cobra defined Hegemony military transport operations for most of the twenty-fourth century and established the tilt-rotor transport template that would echo through centuries of successor designs.

The Cobra VTOL Transport uses an internal combustion engine driving a tilt-rotor assembly for propulsion, achieving a cruise speed of approximately 130 kilometers per hour. While this performance lagged behind faster VTOL designs of the period, the Cobra's strength lay in its carrying capacity rather than raw speed. The spacious internal hold accommodates nine tons of cargo and is fitted with three access doors, right, left, and rear, allowing rapid loading and offloading in the field. The cargo bay accepts interchangeable kit packages, allowing units to reconfigure the vehicle for troop transport, medical evacuation, reconnaissance, airborne command post, or VIP duties without dedicated maintenance facilities.

The vehicle also supports a slung load beneath the airframe, extending its utility to delivery of light artillery pieces, small vehicles, or supplemental bulk cargo alongside its internal carry. For self-defense, four machine guns cover multiple arcs and are supported by an advanced fire control system to improve crew targeting effectiveness under operational conditions. BAR-6 composite armor provides adequate protection for a transport operating in contested airspace, though the Cobra relies primarily on speed and escort for survivability in active combat environments. A three-person crew handles flight, vehicle operations, and gunnery during missions.

The Cobra VTOL Transport's development came at a defining moment in Terran Hegemony history. Director-General James McKenna's rise to power inaugurated a new era of military standardization across what had been the loosely organized Alliance Global Militia. Prior to McKenna's reforms, equipment procurement had been inconsistent at best, with contracts regularly awarded for designs already rejected by the military hierarchy. The Cobra was among the earliest products of the new mandate requiring uniform standards, with Pacific-Euro Consolidated Aerospace Systems receiving the production contract and beginning manufacture in 2317.

The design proved an immediate success and remained the standard Hegemony VTOL transport for most of the twenty-fourth century. Field conversion kits developed in parallel with the original model allowed individual Cobras to be rapidly reconfigured for medical evacuation, airborne command posts, VIP transport, and reconnaissance missions without factory support. The design's adaptability encouraged a continuous stream of specialized configurations, and hundreds of examples entered service across all branches of Hegemony forces. Many decommissioned Cobras eventually found their way into civilian hands, serving government agencies, commercial operators, and the civilian aftermarket as workhorses for nearly every conceivable transport purpose.

By the latter decades of the twenty-fourth century, advancing aerospace technology and the introduction of more capable designs had begun displacing the original Cobra in front-line service. The final military production orders, fulfilled in 2489, incorporated a fusion power plant that improved performance margins and extended the design's useful service life before the original line was discontinued entirely. The Cobra VTOL Transport did not survive to witness the founding of the Star League, but its influence persisted in Hegemony operational records and engineering documentation that directly informed Aldis Industries' development of the Star League-era Cobra Transport VTOL. The tilt-rotor transport concept the Cobra pioneered would prove remarkably enduring, with echoes of its basic design philosophy visible in transport VTOLs produced centuries later across the Inner Sphere.

The Cormorant Medium Cargo Craft is a seventy-ton Wing-in-Ground-Effect transport manufactured by the Michaelson Aircraft division of Michaelson Heavy Industries on Ruchbah since 2690. Developed for the ocean worlds of the Federated Suns, the Cormorant addresses a persistent logistical gap in commercial shipping: while air transport offers speed, its cost makes bulk cargo movement prohibitive over long oceanic distances, and conventional surface shipping lacks the speed and flexibility operators need. The Cormorant occupies the middle ground, skimming ocean surfaces faster than conventional freighters while remaining economical enough for routine cargo operations. Fully amphibious and capable of operating without a prepared airstrip, the craft proves equally suited to established port facilities and remote frontier destinations where infrastructure is minimal. Its rear cargo hatch and large hold have made it one of the most common medium WiGEs in the Federated Suns.

The Cormorant relies on an internal combustion engine for propulsion, giving it a cruise speed suitable for extended ocean crossings while keeping operating costs manageable compared to fusion-powered alternatives. Its rear cargo hatch allows rapid loading and unloading without specialized port equipment, and cargo secured with parachutes and flotation devices can be jettisoned in flight if circumstances demand. The amphibious chassis modification lets the Cormorant operate on water surfaces as well as in ground-effect flight, extending its reach to destinations where dedicated landing facilities are absent.

For protection, the Cormorant carries a pair of machine guns in wing-mounted positions, providing limited deterrence against wildlife and light pirate threats. Its BAR 6 armor offers adequate protection for a commercial platform but leaves the craft vulnerable to organized military opposition. The Cormorant's fundamental weakness is its civilian heritage: designed around cargo volume and economical operation rather than survivability, it performs best when escorts or military assets handle serious threats. Crews operating in contested or wilderness environments have been known to remove the weapons entirely to increase cargo capacity, a trade-off that reflects the tension between commercial efficiency and the realities of operating on worlds where not all dangers are human in origin.

The Terran Hegemony's experimentation with Wing-in-Ground-Effect vehicles during the twenty-fourth century established the technological foundation for designs like the Cormorant, though early Hegemony WiGEs such as the Thorizer proved unsuitable for military applications and saw limited adoption. Michaelson Aircraft, better known for its military aerospace designs, recognized the civilian transport potential of WiGE technology and began developing a purpose-built cargo variant optimized for the ocean worlds becoming increasingly important to the Federated Suns economy. The Cormorant entered production in 2690 at Michaelson's Ruchbah facility and quickly established itself as the workhorse of oceanic cargo logistics throughout the Federated Suns.

Ulysses became the craft's most prominent operational theater, its vast oceans offering both the reach the Cormorant was designed to exploit and hazards its crews had to manage. Large predators, including the Ulysses Tiger Raptor, presented a constant threat to both flight operations and surface cargo handling, giving a distinctly non-military dimension to crew safety procedures. Cormorant crews developed informal tactics for deterring wildlife, and the machine gun installations standard on commercial versions reflected practical necessity as much as anti-piracy concerns.

The Ruchbah facility changed hands repeatedly through the Succession Wars, passing from Terran Hegemony control through an independent period and into Capellan Confederation ownership before the Federated Suns recaptured the system. The Cormorant's fundamental utility kept production largely continuous despite these transitions, and the design accumulated a substantial operational record across multiple political eras. The FedCom Civil War brought intensified piracy to Ulyssean shipping lanes, creating demand for a dedicated military variant that ultimately led Michaelson to develop the Fulmar patrol derivative.

shared: The Dreadnought Mk II Land Train is a military conversion of the Gienah-DuraPaq Elite Series 3 civilian land train, developed by Marian Arms, Inc. on Alphard for the Marian Hegemony Armed Forces. Authorized by Hegemony Armed Forces commander Michael Alexander and supervised by Marian Arms technician Proculeius Lodi, the project sought to transform the Hegemony's essential ore transport vehicles into self-defending convoy platforms capable of protecting critical supply routes without diverting dedicated combat assets to escort duty. Development began in 3072 and formal introduction was achieved in 3081. Consisting of a heavily armed tractor module and a series of interchangeable armed trailer configurations, the Mk II represents one of the Hegemony's most ambitious military engineering efforts. Only two complete trains were ever constructed, making the Dreadnought Mk II among the rarest vehicles in Periphery service.

Each Dreadnought Mk II trailer is an unpowered 50-ton tracked module towed and powered by the tractor unit. The modules draw motive power directly from the tractor's fusion engine, requiring no independent power plant of their own. Built on a commercial Elite Series 3 trailer chassis upgraded with Tech D armor, each module carries four and a half tons of commercial grade ATC armor rated at BAR 7, substantially heavier than the civilian baseline. The modules are interconnectable, allowing the train to be assembled in varying consists by linking modules to each other as well as directly to the tractor.

Each module carries a twenty-ton cargo bay with four access doors on the front, left, right, and rear sides. The cargo carried varies by configuration, with each trailer variant equipped for a specific type of freight. Trailer gunners are quartered aboard the tractor and move to their stations when action is called. All weapon systems are governed by Advanced Fire Control. Individual modules are regularly exchanged between Train 838 and Train 520, allowing the two trains to vary their weapon fits and cargo assignments as mission requirements change across Alphard's mining routes.

The Marian Hegemony's overland transport network has been essential to its economy since the realm's founding, with land trains ferrying ore from Alphard's distant mining fields to Nova Roma and the industrial centers supporting Marian military power. The Gienah-DuraPaq Elite Series 3 became the standard platform for this role, and by the mid-thirty-first century the Hegemony operated substantial convoys of these vehicles across Alphard's varied terrain. As the Hegemony grew from a mining operation into a Periphery power attracting raider interest, the vulnerability of these lightly defended convoys became an increasing liability.

The Word of Blake's terrorist attacks on Nova Roma in the 3060s disrupted supply shipments and rendered several convoy routes untenable. When the Blakists returned the following year and Lugdunum became a primary target, the Hegemony found itself unable to spare military assets for convoy escort. Caesar Cassius O'Reilly's response upon assuming the throne was to appoint Proculeius Lodi of Marian Arms to develop a permanent solution, commissioning a full military conversion of the Elite Series 3 platform rather than relying on improvised escort arrangements.

Lodi's program, begun in 3072, worked closely with HAF commander Michael Alexander to develop specifications for what would become the Dreadnought Mk II. In September 3079, O'Reilly met with Lodi and Alexander in closed session, reviewed the progress of the project, and approved an ambitious upgrade to the design's defensive and offensive capabilities. O'Reilly provided a generous development budget, reflecting the strategic importance the Hegemony placed on protecting its mining infrastructure.

By the late 3070s the Mk II was undergoing field trials on Alphard, with life returning to normal in the Hegemony as the two prototype trains demonstrated the viability of the armed land train concept. Train 838 and Train 520 completed their trials and entered service in 3081. FrontierTech marketed the design as both a military asset and a commercial investment opportunity for potential outside customers, though no additional units beyond the two original trains were confirmed constructed.
Marian Arms, Inc. Tech D Chassis

The Estevez was an eighty-ton tracked main battle tank produced by Novais Motors on New Avalon, named for a popular local militia officer. Introduced in 2310, it was one of the earliest effective armored fighting vehicles developed outside the Terran Hegemony. The design predated the formal founding of the Federated Suns by several years, serving the disparate political entities on New Avalon that would eventually coalesce into the young nation. Its combination of thick armor, substantial firepower, and imposing physical presence made the Estevez the dominant main battle tank in the region throughout the twenty-fourth century. The vehicle's sheer size and power earned it a fearsome reputation among its contemporaries, as lighter armed opponents often chose to retreat rather than engage the massive tank head-on.

Powered by the NM/750 Combat Diesel engine, the Estevez could reach a maximum speed of fifty-four kilometers per hour, competitive with many lighter tanks of its era despite the vehicle's eighty-ton mass. The tank's primary armament consisted of a turret-mounted Avalon Slugger Heavy Rifle, a large-caliber weapon that delivered punishing hits against contemporary targets. Seven tons of stored ammunition gave the Estevez exceptional battlefield endurance, though this massive magazine also represented a significant vulnerability, as a single penetrating hit risked detonating the entire stockpile. Two coaxial PC-50 machine guns and a pair of vehicular grenade launchers provided secondary defense against infantry threats.

Ten and a half tons of Nova-IV Hyper-Composite with Diamond Flex armor gave the Estevez robust protection for its time, rated at BAR 8 across all facings. The Valiant Echo Mk. II communications system and Thermoscan Optics fire control system were adequate for the early twenty-fourth century but grew increasingly outmatched as military technology advanced. The vehicle required a crew of nine, including two officers, two enlisted crew, and five gunners, a substantial manpower requirement that complicated logistics. The design's fuel-thirsty diesel engine further strained supply lines, limiting operational range relative to more efficient contemporaries.

The Fulmar Patrol Craft is a seventy-ton military derivative of the Cormorant, introduced by Michaelson Aircraft in 3056 to meet growing demand for dedicated maritime patrol and convoy escort capability in the Federated Suns. Outwardly similar to its commercial parent, the Fulmar incorporates advanced composite materials that simultaneously improve armor protection and increase top speed, making it noticeably faster and more durable than the cargo craft it was designed to protect. Where the Cormorant prioritizes cargo volume and economy, the Fulmar trades payload space for military systems suited to anti-piracy operations, coastal patrol, and the paramilitary transport of infantry forces. Its introduction coincided with an escalating piracy crisis on Ulysses that would ultimately define the design's early operational reputation.

The Fulmar's advanced composite construction yields armor rated at BAR 8, a significant improvement over the Cormorant's commercial-grade protection, while reducing hull weight enough to accommodate a more powerful drive configuration that raises cruise and flank speeds substantially. This combination of better protection and higher speed makes the Fulmar considerably more capable as an escort and patrol platform than any modified Cormorant hull could achieve.

Armament centers on a pair of light machine guns in wing-mounted positions, supplemented by an Advanced Fire Control system that improves accuracy against the small, fast targets typical of piracy operations. Four mine dispensers mounted to the rear provide area-denial capability useful for blocking coastal approaches and discouraging pursuit by surface vessels. The reduced cargo bay retains sufficient capacity to transport a full company of marines with their equipment, giving the Fulmar practical utility as a paramilitary transport in addition to its patrol role.

The ICE powerplant keeps operating costs manageable for sustained patrol duty. The Fulmar's primary limitation is firepower: the light machine guns and mine dispensers are effective against unarmored or lightly armored smuggler craft but provide limited capability against opponents with meaningful armor protection. The design performs best as a deterrent and pursuit platform against civilian-grade threats rather than a combat vessel expected to engage organized military opposition directly.

Michaelson Aircraft developed the Fulmar in direct response to conditions on Ulysses, where the FedCom Civil War created an environment that coastal pirates and smugglers exploited aggressively. With the Ulyssean Navy's resources stretched by competing demands, shipping losses in the planet's shallow coastal seas reached epidemic proportions as organized pirate groups used their own WiGEs to prey on unescorted cargo craft. The Cormorant's commercial-grade systems were inadequate for self-defense against coordinated attacks, and the scale of losses threatened the planetary economy.

Rather than designing a purpose-built military WiGE from scratch, Michaelson adapted the proven Cormorant hull with advanced composite materials, a strengthened drive system, and military-grade electronics. The Fulmar entered service in 3056 with standard machine gun armament closely resembling its cargo parent, but an updated configuration introduced in 3065 replaced those weapons with light machine guns, added an Advanced Fire Control system, and incorporated rear-mounted mine dispensers for area denial. This configuration proved decisive in addressing the Ulyssean piracy problem.

The Ulysses Navy deployed Fulmars in convoy escort, establishing protective formations around commercial Cormorant flights and gradually forcing pirates to seek softer targets elsewhere. Intelligence gathered through sustained patrol operations eventually identified the primary pirate base on the island of Penelope. A Fulmar squadron transported a full battalion of marines directly to the island, and the resulting assault eliminated the threat. The operation became something of a showcase for the design's dual utility as both patrol platform and military transport. The Fulmar subsequently attracted attention from smugglers themselves, who recognized that a fast, amphibious WiGE with military-grade systems served their purposes as effectively as the naval patrols it was designed to counter.

The Generic Expandable Services Vehicle, commonly known as the GESV, is a multipurpose wheeled support platform developed by the Federated Suns and introduced in 3066. Built around OmniVehicle technology, the design can be rapidly reconfigured to serve virtually any rear-echelon role, from mobile command post to field kitchen to frontline medical facility. The platform serves military units, government agencies, police forces, and civilian relief organizations operating in field environments. Its purpose-built trailer extends the tractor's capabilities further, offering additional configurations for personnel housing and cargo transport. The GESV's design philosophy emphasizes adaptability over specialization, allowing any organization engaged in extended field operations to meet diverse support needs with a single standardized platform rather than a fleet of dedicated vehicles. This flexibility, combined with straightforward maintenance requirements, has made the design a common sight in Federated Suns rear-echelon formations.

The GESV tractor is a medium wheeled support vehicle powered by a fuel cell engine. The fuel cell system eliminates dependence on volatile liquid fuels, reducing the logistical burden in forward areas and improving fire safety when the vehicle is configured as a medical unit or command post. The engine provides sufficient speed to keep pace with most mechanized formations, and the vehicle carries enough fuel for a range of approximately 2,700 kilometers.

Two tons of commercial-grade armor rated at BAR 7 protect the crew and internal equipment against light weapons fire and battlefield debris. This protection level is adequate for a support platform operating behind the front lines, though it provides little security against direct combat engagement. The GESV carries no integral weapons, leaving defense entirely to escort forces or crew personal arms, which is a meaningful limitation in fluid operational environments.

As an OmniVehicle, the GESV dedicates eleven tons of pod space to mission equipment, enabling installation of any combination of modules within that weight limit. A crew of two operates the vehicle itself, with configuration-specific personnel added as required. The tractor can pull up to two purpose-built trailers simultaneously, substantially multiplying available support capacity without additional prime movers. The trade-off for this flexibility is entirely in the vehicle's lack of self-defense capability.

The GESV emerged from a Federated Suns initiative to standardize rear-echelon support infrastructure. By the mid-3060s, the complexities of operating across multiple theaters had exposed the limitations of specialized support vehicles. Different organizations fielded incompatible equipment, creating maintenance and logistics complications that impaired operational efficiency across extended campaigns.

The OmniVehicle architecture provided the engineering solution. By applying the same modular technology used in OmniMechs to a wheeled support platform, engineers produced a vehicle that could be refitted between missions to serve whichever role was most needed. The tractor's eleven tons of pod space accommodated a command post module, a field kitchen, or a MASH unit, while the companion trailer expanded capacity for bunking, cargo, or workspace needs.

Introduced in 3066, the GESV entered service during the final years of the FedCom Civil War. Its timing proved fortunate, as the conflict generated exactly the kind of extended, multi-role operational demand the design was built to address. AFFS rear-echelon units quickly adopted the platform, and its reputation for versatility spread beyond the Federated Suns. Civilian agencies, police departments, and non-governmental relief organizations operating in conflict zones began acquiring the vehicle as well.

The GESV's generic specifications and civilian-grade components allowed manufacturers across the Inner Sphere to produce the vehicle with minimal tooling investment. This distributed production base contributed to the platform's resilience during the Jihad era, when targeted industrial strikes disrupted dedicated combat vehicle lines while GESV production continued at secondary and civilian facilities with little interruption.

The GESV Trailer is a fifteen-ton OmniVehicle designed as a dedicated companion to the GESV tractor. Built on an Omni chassis, the trailer is protected by one and a half tons of BAR 7 armor, sufficient to shield cargo and occupants against incidental fire and debris during rear-echelon operations. The trailer carries no engine of its own, relying entirely on the tractor for movement.

The trailer's OmniVehicle architecture provides full reconfiguration flexibility within available pod space. Unlike traditional cargo or personnel trailers, which commit to a single function from manufacture, the GESV Trailer's interior can be arranged into virtually any configuration that fits within tonnage limits. This makes the platform adaptable to shifting operational priorities without requiring different trailer types in the logistics chain.

Two GESV Trailers can be coupled and pulled simultaneously by a single tractor, allowing commanders to combine functions, such as pairing bunk space with a workspace module, to support diverse unit requirements from a single prime mover. The principal limitation of the trailer is its complete dependence on the tractor for mobility. Without the tractor, the trailer is stationary, which makes initial positioning decisions critical in dynamic operational environments.

The Hector Road Train Trailer Module is an 80-ton wheeled cargo and passenger transport unit designed to be towed by the Hector Road Train Tractor or compatible prime movers. Introduced in 2500 as the cargo-carrying component of the integrated Hector Road Train system, the trailer module is defined by its configurable interior. Five distinct internal arrangements allow the same structural chassis to serve as a dry bulk carrier, liquid tanker, refrigerated goods transport, livestock hauler, or passenger module. Up to two trailer modules may be coupled to a single tractor, with performance reductions applied as load increases. The system's flexibility made the trailer module a practical commercial investment, allowing operators to serve varied cargo requirements with a common hull. Trailer modules spread throughout the Free Worlds League and beyond alongside the Hector Tractor.

The Trailer Module carries no independent propulsion, relying entirely on the tractor for movement. Its structural mass of 80 tons includes 12 tons allocated to chassis and control systems and 1 ton of BAR 3 armor, with the remaining capacity dedicated to the selected cargo or passenger configuration. The chassis uses a tractor/trailer control arrangement that couples mechanically to the prime mover. BAR 3 armor provides 34 armor factor points in a civilian protection standard appropriate to road transport operations, offering basic coverage against minor hazards. The unit has no weapons and no independent movement capability.

The five configurations cover the primary commercial cargo categories. The standard cargo version carries 67 tons of dry bulk goods, accessed through four side doors. The liquid cargo version holds 60.5 tons of fluid freight in a sealed tank, with four access points for pumping equipment. The refrigerated cargo version carries 58 tons of temperature-sensitive goods using active cooling systems, also with four doors. The livestock version accommodates 55.5 tons of live animals in appropriate transport housing with four access doors. The passenger module installs three field kitchens, eleven infantry compartments for up to 308 passengers, and five tons of standard cargo space, with three access doors on the left, right, and rear. All configurations use the same basic structural chassis, simplifying cross-fleet maintenance and allowing mixed configuration convoys.

Irian manufacturers developed the trailer module system in parallel with the Hector Tractor as an integrated logistics solution. Offering five configurations at introduction reflected a deliberate commercial strategy: by covering the primary cargo categories in a single chassis family, the system gave commercial operators a reason to standardize on the Hector rather than purchasing separate purpose-built vehicles. The approach proved effective, and the Hector trailer became the default cargo module for road train operations across much of the Free Worlds League.

The passenger module variant saw particularly broad adoption on frontier worlds where public transit infrastructure was absent or underdeveloped. Operators running Hector passenger trains on scheduled routes between settlements could move over 300 passengers per run, filling a gap between expensive air travel and absent rail service. Some planetary governments contracted Hector passenger services as a managed transit solution, outsourcing public transport to commercial road train operators. Military logistics commands also employed the passenger module for troop movement and dependent transport during peacetime garrison rotations.

The Succession Wars affected trailer module availability through attrition rather than targeted destruction. Modules wore out, suffered accidents, and were cannibalized for parts when repairs became impractical. Local workshops on many worlds developed the capability to fabricate replacement structural components, keeping operational modules running long past their designed service lives. The refrigerated and liquid cargo variants proved particularly durable in commercial service, because the industries they supported, food distribution and fuel transport, remained economically essential regardless of political conditions.

By the Renaissance era, Hector trailer modules in various states of modification remained in service on dozens of worlds. The configurability that defined the original design proved equally useful across its long service life, as operators modified interior arrangements to suit local requirements. Some workshops fabricated configurations not in the original specification using the basic chassis structure. The trailer module's legacy was ultimately one of practical endurance, a flexible design that outlasted the industrial context that produced it.

The Hesiod Utility Vehicle is a civilian ultralight OmniVehicle introduced in 3060 by Earthwerks-FWL, Incorporated as a cost-effective alternative to fixed-configuration utility equipment. Leveraging OmniVehicle technology traditionally reserved for military applications, Earthwerks offered the Hesiod as a single platform capable of fulfilling multiple specialized roles through interchangeable working modules. The vehicle found immediate interest across the Inner Sphere, appealing to colonial administrators and agricultural operators looking to reduce fleet costs without sacrificing operational flexibility.

Its alcohol-fueled engine, off-road chassis, and modest footprint made it well-suited to frontier and developing-world environments where road infrastructure was limited and budget constraints were constant. Despite its civilian focus, the Hesiod proved adaptable enough that later configurations would extend its service into militarized support roles as well.

Earthwerks-FWL, Incorporated introduced the Hesiod Utility Vehicle in 3060 from its manufacturing facility on Bernardo, capitalizing on civilian demand for modular equipment that had grown alongside the Inner Sphere's post-Clan Invasion economic recovery. The design drew on OmniVehicle technology originally developed for military applications, adapting it to a cost-effective civilian platform accessible to colonial governments and agricultural cooperatives.

Initial sales were strong, with the Hesiod gaining buyers throughout the Inner Sphere. The Bernardo plant could not keep pace with demand, and Earthwerks eventually outsourced some production to its Capellan Confederation facilities. This decision triggered friction at the Bernardo plant, where workers staged strikes and circulated claims that the Capellan-built vehicles were substandard. Earthwerks maintained publicly that quality controls across all facilities were uniform, but the labor disputes and rumors persisted, complicating sales in some markets.

The FedCom Civil War proved damaging to Hesiod sales in the Federated Suns and Lyran space from the mid-3060s onward, cutting off a significant customer base and leaving the Free Worlds League as the primary revenue source. The vehicle survived these pressures and continued in production through subsequent political changes on Bernardo, which passed through Republic of the Sphere and Senate Alliance jurisdiction before returning to Free Worlds League control.

During the Jihad, Earthwerks released a weapons module for the platform carrying four Light Machine Guns, allowing the Hesiod to serve in rear-area militia and security roles. This development reflected the broader militarization of civilian platforms that characterized the era, when any available vehicle with weapons potential was pressed into service.

The Hesiod's most significant technical feature is its OmniVehicle chassis, which provides three tons of OmniPod space for swapping between four distinct working modules. The 7-ton frame rides on an off-road wheeled chassis that handles unpaved terrain reliably, though the vehicle is not intended for high-speed operation. Its ICE engine delivers a cruise speed of 40 km/h and a top speed of 60 km/h, drawing on a 2,666 km range from its alcohol fuel supply. That extended range allows the vehicle to operate independently of fuel logistics for extended periods, a practical necessity on frontier worlds.

All configurations carry commercial armor at BAR 4, offering environmental protection against the elements but minimal resistance to deliberate weapons fire. The Hesiod is unarmed in its baseline configurations, and its crew of two enlisted operators shares the cab regardless of which module is installed.

The vehicle's principal limitation is its single-configuration operation. Swapping OmniPods requires ground crew support and downtime, meaning the flexibility advantage of the platform is realized across a deployment rather than moment to moment. Operators who expect to reconfigure frequently will need logistics support unavailable in austere frontier conditions. The light construction also limits the Hesiod to civilian workloads; it is not suited to heavy-duty operations alongside large construction equipment.

The Ibex RV is a two-ton wheeled utility vehicle introduced in 3049 by Earthwerks-FWL, Incorporated, designed to serve farmers and rural settlers across the Free Worlds League's more rugged worlds. Rugged, reliable, and capable off-road, the design quickly gained broader appeal far beyond its original agricultural market, becoming a fixture in urban centers where its oversized form and commanding presence made it a peculiar status symbol among the social elite. Law enforcement agencies and Free Worlds League Militia units also recognized its practical utility, adopting the platform for light patrol and security duties. A militarized variant followed almost immediately, adding heavier armor and light weaponry without fundamentally altering the vehicle's core character as a tough, go-anywhere utility truck.

The Ibex RV is built around a wheeled off-road chassis and powered by an internal combustion engine with a 500-kilometer range on its eleven-kilogram fuel tank. Civilian versions carry BAR 4 armor, sufficient for industrial hazards but not designed to stop weapons fire. The vehicle accommodates eight occupants including the driver, accessed through two side doors per side and a rear entry, making it well-suited for transporting small work teams across rough terrain. Its 601-kilogram cargo bay handles tools, equipment, and supplies for extended fieldwork.

The militarized version upgrades armor protection to BAR 7, adding meaningful resistance against light weapons fire. The initial military variant mounts twin King David man-pack Gauss rifles in a pintle arrangement, while the later Gauss variant places side-mounted King David light Gauss rifles for improved standoff capability. Neither variant is intended for frontline combat, but both provide security personnel and militia forces with a credible deterrent against unarmored threats and light opposition. The reduction in cargo capacity on the militarized version to 388 kilograms is a meaningful trade-off for operators who rely on the platform for logistics as well as security.

Earthwerks-FWL, Incorporated introduced the Ibex RV in 3049, targeting the agricultural and rural communities that define much of the Free Worlds League's settlement patterns on its less-developed worlds. The design filled a genuine gap in the civilian utility market, offering a capable off-road vehicle with sufficient cargo capacity and passenger room to serve as a farm workhorse, a community transport, and a light logistics platform for rural businesses.

Demand spread quickly beyond the fields. The Ibex's imposing size and rugged character attracted urban buyers who valued its image as much as its capability. In League cities, the trucks became familiar sights driven by security executives, corporate managers, and others seeking to project an image of active, self-reliant outdoor living. The gap between that aspiration and the reality of commuting and school runs earned the design the affectionate nickname of "snob tractors" among those who noted the irony of farm vehicles navigating city streets. Security services took a more practical view, appreciating the platform's durability and load capacity for patrol and perimeter work.

Recognizing the military potential of the existing chassis, Earthwerks-FWL introduced the Militarized variant alongside the base model in 3049, adding heavier armor and twin King David man-pack Gauss rifles to equip militia and security forces. The Free Worlds League Militia integrated the type into light patrol and support roles on numerous member worlds. In 3064, a second militarized configuration replaced the pintle-mounted weapons with permanently fixed side-mounted King David light Gauss rifles, providing improved accuracy and greater standoff range for units operating in contested environments.

The JI-50 Transportable Field Repair Unit, commonly known as the Jifty, is a Federated Suns support vehicle designed to bring repair and recovery capabilities directly to damaged units in the field. Manufactured by Johnston Industries on New Syrtis, the 60-ton tracked vehicle entered service in 3069 as an evolution of earlier field repair concepts pioneered by the Free Worlds League's Paramour MRV. The Jifty's combination of heavy cargo capacity, lift hoists, and fusion-powered mobility makes it a valuable force multiplier for military formations operating beyond the reach of fixed repair facilities. Its versatile chassis has spawned numerous field modifications adapted to the demands of frontline service during the Jihad.

The Jifty's fusion engine drives the 60-ton tracked vehicle at a cruising speed of 32 kph with a flank speed of 48 kph. Its tracked motive system was selected to handle the rough terrain typically encountered when recovering damaged vehicles and BattleMechs. A pair of lift hoists mounted at the front can each handle loads of up to 60 tons, enabling the Jifty to manipulate and recover even assault-class BattleMechs. The vehicle carries 19.5 tons of cargo in an internal bay with a rear access door, providing ample space for spare parts, tools, and salvaged components.

Protection comes from 3.5 tons of industrial-grade BAR 6 armor, reflecting the vehicle's intended role behind the front lines rather than in direct combat. A pair of light machine guns provide minimal self-defense against infantry and unarmored threats, operated by two of the vehicle's four crew members. The Jifty is not designed for combat and relies on escorting forces for protection in contested areas. Its primary value lies in reducing the time and distance required to return damaged equipment to operational status, keeping combat formations at higher readiness than would otherwise be possible.

Johnston Industries developed the Jifty at their New Syrtis facility, drawing heavily on design features from the Free Worlds League's Paramour MRV. The vehicle entered production in 3069, coinciding with the opening stages of the Jihad. Johnston's timing proved both fortunate and unfortunate. The desperate need for field repair capability during the widespread fighting ensured immediate demand, but the conflicts raging across the Federated Suns also threatened the factory itself.

The Capellan Confederation's Operation Thunderstrike in 3069 brought fighting to New Syrtis and the surrounding Capellan March worlds. While Johnston Industries' security forces helped the Fourth Donegal Guards defend the factory complex, the broader invasion spread captured Jiftys into Capellan hands. The Taurian Concordat similarly recovered nearly a dozen from Davion forces around the Pleiades Cluster during their 3067 incursion. These captures gave neighboring powers access to a vehicle that had been exclusively Federated Suns equipment.

By 3069, Johnston Industries had begun granting limited manufacturing licenses to smaller companies outside the Capellan March, recognizing that demand far exceeded what a single factory could supply during wartime. This expansion of production ensured the Jifty's wider adoption across the Inner Sphere, though the Federated Suns remained its primary operator. The various field modifications that emerged during the Jihad reflected the creativity of technicians adapting the vehicle to rapidly changing battlefield requirements.

The fighting on New Syrtis during the Jihad devastated the Johnston Industries facility in Cilitren on the continent of Mawreddog. The factory was heavily damaged, and the surrounding city was effectively destroyed. Johnston responded by expanding its facilities on Benet III to recover lost production capacity, though plans to restart at least partial production on New Syrtis continued throughout the rebuilding period. The damage to Johnston's primary facility had ripple effects across the company's entire product line, affecting production of vehicles far beyond the Jifty.

The corporate sphere surrounding the Jifty also produced controversy. In the latter half of the 3060s, Blue Bull, Inc. produced a blatant copy of the JI-50 called the "Nifty," an ICE-powered knockoff that undercut the Jifty's market position. Johnston Industries attempted to pursue legal action for patent violations, but the chaos of the Jihad prevented any meaningful progress in the courts. The years since proved Johnston's concerns well-founded. The JI-100, a larger successor to the Jifty introduced in 3074, demonstrated that the original design concept was sound enough to scale upward, and military commands gradually upgraded from the JI-50 to the JI-100 where budgets permitted. The Nifty found no lasting place on Federated Suns equipment rosters.

The Kallon UL-series is a family of industrial construction vehicles introduced in 3054 by Kallon Industries. Designed as affordable, versatile worksite equipment, the series quickly established itself as the benchmark for civilian construction machinery across the Inner Sphere. All four production models share an identical ten-ton tracked chassis with an adjustable-height suspension, differing only in their mounted construction apparatus. Kallon produces the UL-series at multiple facilities across the rimward Inner Sphere, with plants in both the Federated Suns and Free Worlds League fabricating all components onsite. The vehicles are light enough to transport by truck, making them popular with construction firms operating on remote frontier worlds far from established infrastructure.

The UL-series chassis features an innovative adjustable-height design built around hydraulic outriggers mounted on the drive tracks. These outriggers lift the main body above obstacles and allow the vehicle to operate on hillsides or span narrow pits. An automatic leveling sensor tied to an audible alarm ensures stable operation on uneven terrain. The Kallon Growler internal combustion engine provides sufficient torque to drive any of the four available construction attachments, and a half-ton fuel tank gives the vehicles extended operational range without refueling, a strong selling point for companies breaking new ground far from support facilities.

At ten tons, the UL-series is light enough for truck transport, a significant advantage for construction companies working at remote sites. The tracked chassis carries only minimal industrial-grade plating rated to deflect debris rather than weapons fire, offering no meaningful protection in a combat environment. The vehicles mount no weapons and rely entirely on their operators and local site security for defense.

Kallon Industries introduced the UL-series in 3054 to compete in the civilian construction equipment market, a sector where larger firms like Earthwerks Incorporated had established footholds with products such as the Lesseps Dumper line. The series found rapid commercial success across the rimward Inner Sphere, with Kallon factories in the Federated Suns and Free Worlds League producing all four models using entirely onsite-manufactured components. Minor regional variations in weights and measures exist between production facilities, but the core designs remain identical.

Kallon executives have aggressively marketed the vehicles through demonstrations showing UL units clearing debris from burning structures and responding to vehicle accidents. This campaign directly targets Earthwerks, whose own construction equipment supplements have suffered from the poor reputation of the Lesseps Dumper among operators. The strategy has proven effective, allowing Kallon to capture a growing share of the civilian construction market that Earthwerks has struggled to defend.

Lexan Oceanic is a luxury transport manufacturer with roots in the mid-twenty-first century, when the firm designed and decorated high-end properties for the wealthy elite of the Inner Sphere. Under the direction of Corrine Yeardly, the company partnered with Boeing United in 2311 to enter the personal VTOL market. The renamed United Airframe company established production facilities on New Earth and Keid, producing custom aircraft that quickly became status symbols among interstellar corporate executives and nobility.

The original Series II personal VTOL established Lexan's reputation for exclusive, fusion-powered luxury aircraft during the Star League era. The larger Series VI luxury VTOL followed centuries later in 3053, expanding the product line to serve an even more demanding clientele. Both designs cater to the ultra-wealthy, offering unlimited range and bespoke interiors unmatched by any competitor.

The Series II is a medium VTOL weighing fifteen tons, powered by a compact fusion engine that gives it unlimited operational range and impressive speed. One ton of BAR 10 commercial armor provides protection comparable to standard military-grade plating, while a defensive ECM suite makes electronic detection difficult. The aircraft's six-passenger cabin is custom-fitted for each buyer, with exotic materials and appointments unique to every airframe. Foldable wings allow the Series II to be stored in a DropShip cargo bay for convenient interstellar transport.

The Series VI triples the Series II's mass at sixty tons, trading top speed for interior space and amphibious capability. Its fusion engine maintains unlimited range, while the armored and amphibious chassis allows water landings. The VI features first-class quarters, 2.5 tons of BAR 10 armor, and a 1.5-ton cargo capacity. Neither design carries armament of any kind, relying instead on speed, ECM protection, and low observability rather than firepower. The lack of weapons is a deliberate design choice, as any military hardpoints would undermine the craft's civilian certification and insurance classification.

Lexan Oceanic began as a design firm specializing in luxury interiors for the wealthy, decorating everything from penthouse apartments to low-orbit space station suites and custom DropShips. Owning a Lexan product signified power, money, and social position among the Inner Sphere's elite. In 2311, Corrine Yeardly steered the company into aircraft production through a partnership with Boeing United, a small subsidiary of the larger Boeing conglomerate responsible for passenger VTOL production. Using a standard VT-1922 airframe, Lexan provided custom specifications while Boeing United handled construction. The venture proved enormously profitable, and Lexan shareholders eventually acquired Boeing United outright. The newly renamed United Airframe opened factories on New Earth and Keid.

The Series II became a favorite among interstellar corporate leaders during the Star League era. Each aircraft was unique in its appointments, containing such luxuries as Terran redwood floors, Capolla jade filigree, Acamarian diamond strings, and Tharkad coral inlay. The last Series II built before the fall of the original factories was commissioned for Stefan Pretanis, CEO of Earthwerks. Both United Airframe factories were destroyed during the First Succession War by Davion and Steiner troops, ending production for centuries.

Lexan Oceanic survived by returning to interior decoration for the rich and famous. In 3047, CEO Jason Ullman-Yeardly repurchased the New Earth facility from IrTech after IrTech exited the airframe business following a corporate reshuffling. Lexan's R&D division developed the Series VI, a larger and more versatile design three times the size of the Series II. The Series VI entered production in 3053 after a brief delay caused by the Clan Invasion. The most expensive Series VI ever produced was a pair of custom aircraft built for ex-Archon Katrina Steiner in 3066, whose combined customization costs exceeded the base airframe price by 42 million C-bills. Katrina never received her aircraft. Archon Peter Steiner donated them to the Tharkad Make-a-Dream Foundation in September of 3067.

The Paramour Mobile Repair Vehicle was introduced in 2557 by Gilbert, Sachs, and Belafonte, a Tiber-based conglomerate in the Free Worlds League. Designed during the period when the League prepared to join the Star League, the Paramour represented a deliberate strategic choice to invest in logistics rather than direct combat capability. GSB, Inc. applied its expertise in luxury rough-terrain vehicles to create a mobile repair platform that would keep FWLM units operating at peak readiness in the field. The result was a vehicle that combined comfort, reliability, and genuine utility in a sixty-ton tracked chassis. The FWLM was so impressed with the design that it purchased every Paramour produced. Though the vehicle's polished appearance sometimes drew mockery from combat formations, the Paramour earned lasting respect through the competence and professionalism of its crews.

The Paramour is built on a sixty-ton tracked chassis powered by a fusion engine capable of reaching speeds up to 65 km/h. This mobility allows it to keep pace with armored formations while carrying the tools and parts needed for field repairs. The vehicle's primary asset is its spacious cargo area, which holds fifteen tons of spare parts and equipment for a wide variety of maintenance tasks. A pair of lift hoists enables the Paramour to handle loads up to sixty tons each, sufficient to lift and reposition damaged BattleMechs or heavy combat vehicles on the battlefield.

The crew compartment accommodates three personnel, with quarters comfortable enough to serve as a mobile field headquarters for quartermasters. A five-ton infantry bay provides space for additional technicians or a security detail. For self-defense, the vehicle mounts a single GM MiniGun machine gun in the front, providing a visible deterrent without adding excessive weight. BAR 6 armor offers adequate protection against small arms fire and shrapnel, while the armored chassis and controls modification provides additional resilience. The Paramour was never intended to see direct combat, and its light armament reflects that design philosophy.

The Free Worlds League commissioned the Paramour in the mid-twenty-sixth century as part of a broader effort to bring the FWLM up to Star League Defense Force standards. League planners recognized that matching the SLDF in firepower was impractical, and instead focused on logistical excellence as a way to demonstrate institutional competence. Gilbert, Sachs, and Belafonte, a conglomerate better known for building exotic excursion vehicles for wealthy Free Worlders, won the production contract. The company's experience with luxury vehicles translated into an unusually refined design for a military support platform.

During the Star League era, duty aboard a Paramour became a prestigious assignment within the FWLM. Quartermasters routinely established their field headquarters aboard the vehicles, and daily inspections of crew areas and uniforms became standard practice. This attention to presentation drew scorn from visiting SLDF officers, who dismissed the Paramour crews as more concerned with appearance than function. The reputation proved unfair. When called upon to service combat units in the field, Paramour crews consistently delivered high-quality work that eventually won over even their harshest critics.

GSB, Inc. did not survive the Second Succession War, and production of the Paramour ceased permanently. Although the vehicles were rigorously maintained wherever they served, attrition and entropy gradually thinned the ranks of functional examples over the following centuries.

The Jihad and the collapse of federal authority brought renewed attention to surviving Paramours. Two vehicles appeared on Regulus, where they were reconditioned for service with the Regulan Hussars. By replacing the quarters and cargo space with a mobile field base, the Hussars transformed the Paramour into a true repair vehicle suited to sustained independent operations. The Regulan Prince's intentions for deploying these rare vehicles remained a subject of speculation.

The Prime Mover is not a single designed vehicle but a broad classification of large wheeled logistics platforms that have supported military operations across the Inner Sphere for centuries. First recorded in Inner Sphere inventories around 2420, these six-wheeled fusion-powered trucks share common features, including a cabover cab, an integrated flatbed, and a rear cargo bay, rather than a shared blueprint. Multiple manufacturers across every major state and many Periphery worlds independently developed compatible designs, resulting in a vehicle class united by operational requirements rather than common production. The Prime Mover's ability to haul up to twenty tons of cargo over cross-country terrain without refueling stops made it indispensable to military logistics from the Age of War onward. Though designed as a civilian hauler, modest defensive armament and sturdy construction drew military operators to the platform, and prime movers have served line armies, garrison forces, and irregular units with equal reliability across every era of Inner Sphere history.

The standard Prime Mover is built around a cabover-style crew cab with two small lasers mounted on either side, connected to a large integrated flatbed rated for twenty tons of cargo. A rear-mounted SRM-4 provides additional defensive firepower, operated by the vehicle's cargo handler, who serves as the third crew member alongside the driver and a cab gunner. Advanced Fire Control improves weapons accuracy beyond what is typical for a logistics vehicle, giving the Prime Mover genuine defensive capability against light infantry and vehicles.

The fusion power plant eliminates range limitations that would otherwise constrain logistics operations, allowing prime movers to sustain forward supply chains without fuel depots. Six tons of commercial armor, rated at BAR 7, provides limited protection against small arms and light fragmentary threats, but the design was never intended to absorb sustained weapons fire. The off-road chassis and six-wheel drive allow it to follow combat forces through broken terrain that would stop conventional trucks, though ground speed is moderate. The design's three-man crew allows simultaneous cargo operations and weapons management, but the requirement to crew both cab mounts and the rear launcher demands coordination under fire. The Prime Mover's main weakness is its bulk, which reduces maneuverability and makes it a large target for heavier weapons.

Fusion-powered heavy trucks capable of sustained cross-country operations emerged from multiple manufacturing centers during the early Age of War, driven by the need to move hazardous or heavy cargo independently of fuel supply chains. By approximately 2420, the basic configuration of a six-wheeled fusion-powered hauler with an integrated flatbed had coalesced into a broadly recognized vehicle class. No single manufacturer controlled the design, and variants proliferated across every Inner Sphere state and most Periphery territories, sharing operational concepts rather than interchangeable parts.

During the Star League era, prime movers became standard equipment in SLDF logistics trains and planetary garrison inventories. Their operational independence made them essential to sustained campaigning in contested space, where fuel supply could not be guaranteed. The Succession Wars placed severe pressure on fusion-powered vehicles of all kinds, and prime movers were no exception. As fusion engines became scarce, many were stripped from logistics vehicles to keep BattleMechs operational. Units that survived the early wars were often converted to ICE power at considerable cost in range and flexibility, though the vehicles remained in service across all factions in degraded form.

The recovery of lostech during the late Succession Wars and the gradual return of fusion engine availability revitalized prime mover fleets across the Inner Sphere. By the Clan Invasion era, the original fusion-powered configuration had largely been restored in front-line units, while ICE variants remained common in second-line and militia service. Through the Jihad and into the Republic era, roving scavengers and irregular forces came to prize captured prime movers for their operational independence, fueling a secondary market in surplus vehicles and spare parts. The so-called RAMTech job on New Kyoto in 3115 drew public attention when thieves used two dozen prime movers as decoys during a high-profile operation, demonstrating how unremarkable and ubiquitous the vehicle had become. The incident served as a reminder to military planners that a design this common cuts both ways, offering logistics resilience while also providing cover for irregular activities.

The RRV Rock Rover is a light infantry transport half-track produced by Pinard Electric Motors for the Taurian Concordat. Introduced in 2619, the four-ton vehicle was designed to support mechanized conventional infantry formations with reliable on-road and off-road transportation and basic fire support. The Rock Rover is one of the smaller military vehicles in common service, built not for speed but for durability and versatility in its infantry carrier role. Its small size allows it to navigate urban environments and rough terrain that larger combat vehicles cannot easily access, making it a common sight in garrison and second-line formations across the Concordat. The design has also found buyers in civilian security markets across the Periphery and Inner Sphere, demonstrating broad utility beyond purely military applications.

The Rock Rover's half-track drivetrain provides a useful balance of mobility across varied terrain. An electric fuel cell engine delivers modest power sufficient for convoy escort and infantry support operations. The tracked rear section handles difficult ground and open terrain well, while the vehicle's compact profile lets it enter areas that larger platforms cannot negotiate as easily. Cruising and flanking speeds are low, but adequate for keeping pace with dismounted infantry.

For a vehicle of its size, the Rock Rover carries respectable armament. A turret-mounted Magna Red Star support laser serves as the primary weapon, backed by thirty shots of stored power. Two side-mounted auto-rifles in pintle bubble mounts provide additional defensive firepower, each carrying 300 rounds. Advanced fire control gives the crew targeting capability on par with much larger military vehicles. Armor protection is noteworthy for the weight class, with BAR 8 rated plating covering the hull sufficient to resist most small arms fire. The rear cargo bay accommodates up to fourteen unarmored infantry with equipment, while over a ton of general cargo space provides logistical flexibility. Weapon slits along the hull allow embarked troops to fire from within the vehicle even while in motion.

text.overview: The AC/2 Carrier is a sixty-ton tracked combat vehicle designed to provide long-range ballistic fire support at minimal cost. Part of the broader family of weapons carrier vehicles that originated during the Age of War, the AC/2 Carrier dates back to approximately 2520 in its primitive form, with the modernized version entering service alongside its missile carrier cousins. Built by Quikscell and numerous other manufacturers across the Inner Sphere, the vehicle fills a niche as cheap, expendable suppressive fire support, using volume of autocannon fire to compensate for the relatively modest damage output of individual Class 2 weapons.
text.capabilities:
The primitive AC/2 Carrier represents the earliest member of the weapons carrier family to mount ballistic weapons, entering service around 2520. Built as a fifty-five-ton support vehicle using primitive construction methods, it mounts four Class 2 autocannons behind BAR 6 armor with advanced fire control systems that partially compensate for the crude platform.

The design's straightforward maintenance requirements made it accessible to militaries with limited technical infrastructure. These vehicles were rendered obsolete by modernized carriers around 2580 but served through the Age of War era, establishing the ballistic carrier concept alongside the earlier missile carrier designs.
text.deployment: The primitive AC/2 Carrier served during the Age of War, providing long-range ballistic fire support for armies still relying on pre-spaceflight military technology. Quik Products Inc manufactured these vehicles alongside the primitive missile carriers, establishing the full weapons carrier family that would endure for centuries.
text.battleHistory:
The AC/2 Carrier traces its lineage to the Age of War, when Quik Products Inc developed a family of standardized tracked weapons platforms. The primitive ancestor entered service around 2520 mounting four Class 2 autocannons behind BAR 6 armor with advanced fire control systems. Despite crude construction, the design proved effective enough to inspire the modernized version that served through the Star League era and beyond. Like the missile carriers, the AC/2 Carrier suffered from widespread unauthorized copying during the Succession Wars, and Quikscell's post-Fourth Succession War legal campaign shut down many competitors.

Production spread across an extensive network. Quikscell plants on Ares, Kalidasa, Layover, Oliver, Pandora, and Richvale formed the core, supplemented by Hadrian Mechanized Industries on Pompey, Aldis Industries on Terra, Bordello Military Goods on Antwerp, and Joint Equipment Systems on Alshain. This distributed base mirrored the missile carrier network.

The AC/2 Carrier received its first major modernization in 3063 with the LB-X variant. This substantial redesign replaced the internal combustion engine with a fusion powerplant, doubled armor protection, and substituted the standard autocannons with LB-X Class 2 weapons capable of firing both solid slugs and cluster ammunition. A C3 slave computer enabled networked targeting. Quikscell produced the LB-X variant at most of its carrier plants.

Despite its long service history, the AC/2 Carrier has always occupied a somewhat ambiguous position within the weapons carrier family. The vehicle's similarity to the Pike support vehicle has caused persistent identification problems in the field. However, the AC/2 Carrier continues to fill its role as cheap long-range suppressive fire support, its simplicity and low cost ensuring continued relevance.

text.overview: The Adelante is a six-hundred-ton rail tractor developed jointly by Alstom Rail Corporation and Blackwell Corporation in the early 3060s. Conceived as the driving force behind an innovative modular rail system, the Adelante replaced centuries of inefficient switchyard coupling operations with a streamlined approach to long-distance ground transportation. Powered by a massive fusion engine, the tractor hauls one or more of Alstom's interchangeable TGV Omni Railcar trailers across continental rail networks at impressive speeds. Its combination of raw hauling power and compatibility with the omni-configured trailer system made the Adelante an immediate commercial success, attracting buyers across the Inner Sphere. Both civilian freight operators and military logistics commands recognized the platform's potential, leading to widespread adoption that has kept the design in continuous service for decades.
text.capabilities:
